intro: This guide takes your group through Grace Abounding (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter each week. It’s written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. John Bunyan, the tinker who later wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress, wrote this book in prison to tell, plainly and honestly, how God’s grace reached him: from a swearing village ringleader, through years of fear, doubt and torment, to peace in Christ, preaching, and twelve years in Bedford gaol.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand. Talk it through using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about 10 minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper, pens and Bibles. This book needs particular pastoral care. Bunyan describes despair, intrusive and unwanted thoughts, obsessive mental loops, low mood and feeling “weary of my life, and yet afraid to die,” especially in Chapters 6 to 10. Some of your group may recognise themselves in him. Read those chapters ahead, never ask anyone to share their own thoughts or struggles in front of the group, and make it clear that you are available to talk privately. Know where to point a teen for help, including a doctor, a counsellor and a crisis line where you live, and if anyone tells you they are thinking of hurting themselves, act on it straight away.

weeks.summary: Bunyan, born in 1628 to a poor tinker’s family, wrote this book in a Bedford prison to tell plainly how grace reached him. As a boy he was a champion swearer haunted by nightmares of judgment, and as a teenager the ringleader of village wickedness, who survived drowning, an adder and a siege that killed the soldier who took his place, yet none of it changed him. The big idea: fear and close calls don’t change a heart on their own; only grace does.

memory_verse.text: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.

activity.title: Did It Change Anything?
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s verdict: “Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy, but neither of them did awaken my soul to righteousness.”
Discuss why people often go straight back to how they were after a scare or a close call.
Ask everyone to write, for themselves, one sentence about a scare or close call in their own life, and whether it changed anything.
Talk about why Bunyan opens his book with his worst side rather than his best, writing to people who looked up to him.
Read 1 Timothy 1:15 together and ask what “of whom I am the foremost” shows about how Paul and Bunyan saw themselves.

weeks.summary: Newly married and very poor, Bunyan reads two Christian books his wife brought and becomes outwardly religious while keeping his wicked life. A sermon on the Sabbath troubles him only until lunchtime, and that afternoon, in the middle of a game of cat, a voice asks, “Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?” Instead of turning, he decides it is too late and throws himself into sin. The big idea: “it’s too late for me, so why bother” is despair pretending to be honesty, and a question from God means the door is still open.

memory_verse.text: Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.

activity.title: The Too-Late Lie
steps: Write on a board: “I’ve already blown it, so I might as well keep going.”
Ask the group where people their age might hear that thought, such as revision, a training plan, a habit or a friendship, keeping examples general.
Discuss why it feels realistic, and why the chapter calls it a lie.
Together, write three short answers to the lie, each one a small right step someone could take anyway.
Read Isaiah 55:7 and ask what it says to someone who thinks it’s too late.

weeks.summary: Rebuked by a neighbour for his swearing, Bunyan stops almost at once, starts reading the Bible, keeps the Ten Commandments as his way to heaven and enjoys being praised as a changed man. Yet he admits he was “a poor painted hypocrite,” still ignorant of Christ and trying to build his own righteousness, and his fear-filled “what if” thoughts drove him from the bell tower. The big idea: we can look Christian and enjoy the praise while our heart still hasn’t met God.

memory_verse.text: For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.

activity.title: Painted or Real?
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s words about being “a poor painted hypocrite.”
Draw two columns on a board: “What people can see” and “What only God sees.”
Fill them in together with general examples of what a Christian life might look like on the outside and the inside.
Discuss how social media makes it easier than ever to look good while hiding what is really going on.
Challenge everyone to do one good thing this week that nobody sees, and not to mention it to anyone.

weeks.summary: In a Bedford street Bunyan overhears three or four poor women talking joyfully about the new birth and God’s love in Jesus, and realises he knows nothing of it. His heart softens, he keeps returning to listen, and he prays for help to know truth from error, but his anxious mind invents a test of faith with puddles. In a dream he sees himself squeezing through a narrow gap in a wall into the sunshine, the gap being Jesus. The big idea: the way into God’s warmth is a person, Jesus, not proving ourselves, and real joyful faith draws others in.

memory_verse.text: For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.

activity.title: Women in the Sun
steps: Read aloud the description of the women talking “as if joy did make them speak.”
Discuss: why did their conversation affect Bunyan more than an argument would have?
Compare the puddle test with the gap in the wall: one is Bunyan trying to prove himself, the other is God showing him the way in.
Ask everyone to write down privately the name of someone whose faith seems real and joyful to them.
Encourage them to ask that person this week, “How did God first become real to you?”

weeks.summary: Two new fears grip Bunyan: whether God had chosen him, and whether the day of grace was already over for him. A sentence about no one who trusted the Lord being put to shame comforts him, though he later finds it in the Apocrypha and sees it sums up many Bible promises. Then the words of Jesus’ parable, “and yet there is room,” break into his mind and give him hope. The big idea: whatever we fear, Jesus is still inviting people in, and there is still room.

memory_verse.text: And the servant said, “Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.”

activity.title: Still Room at the Table
steps: Read Luke 14:15–24 aloud together.
List who ends up at the table in the story.
Discuss how “What if I’m not chosen?” and “What if I’m too late?” are really the same fear: that there is no place for me.
Talk about times people feel there is no room for them, such as walking into a room where everyone already has a group.
Ask everyone to write the words “and yet there is room” on a card to keep where they’ll see it every day this week.

weeks.summary: Bunyan begins meeting the Bedford Christians and their pastor, John Gifford, but the closer he gets, the more he sees of his own sinful heart, and for years he feels worse than everyone else. He refuses to get rid of guilt by distraction, and a sermon on the words “My love” finally sets his heart burning with assurance that nothing can separate him from Christ’s love, though within forty days he doubts again. The big idea: feelings of God’s love can fade, but that doesn’t make them false, and seeing our sin more clearly can be a sign of life.

memory_verse.text: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

activity.title: Write It Down
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s wish for pen and ink, and his admission that within forty days he began to doubt again.
Discuss why it is so easy to feel that everyone else has a better heart than we do.
Give everyone a few quiet minutes to write down, for themselves, one moment when God’s love felt real to them, with the date.
Read Romans 8:38–39 together and ask which part of the list stands out to them.
Remind the group that if a heavy, hopeless feeling about themselves lasts for weeks, it is wise to talk to a parent, pastor or doctor, and that you are available to talk privately.

weeks.summary: A verse about Satan sifting Peter follows Bunyan, and then a storm comes: floods of blasphemous doubts, a terrible pull to say what he most feared, and horrible thoughts during prayer. He notices that he hates these thoughts, and that hatred shows something in him refuses them. After about a year God brings him out through the peace made by Christ’s blood, Pastor Gifford’s advice, and Luther’s commentary on Galatians. The big idea: a thought you hate is not a thought you chose, and you don’t have to fight such thoughts alone.

memory_verse.text: Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

activity.title: Not Who You Are
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s line: “Only by the distaste that they gave unto my spirit, I felt there was something in me that refused to embrace them.”
Talk together about what the chapter says: unwanted, horrible thoughts are very common, and hating them shows they are not who you are.
Discuss why hiding such thoughts makes them heavier, and why fighting them harder often makes them louder.

As a group, make a list of safe people a teen could talk to, such as a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor or counsellor, and the words they could use to start: “I keep getting horrible thoughts I don’t want.”
Read Luke 22:31–32 and note that Jesus prayed for Peter before the trial came. Remind everyone you are available to talk privately.

weeks.summary: After a time of peace, Bunyan is hammered for a year by a single thought, “sell Christ,” sometimes a hundred times in a row, and he fights it until he is exhausted. One morning a tired thought slips through, “Let Him go, if He will,” and he falls into despair for two years, believing he is like Esau, with only brief breaks such as seeing his sin as a small stone beside the vast field of Christ’s blood. The big idea: a mind locked in a loop is not proof that you are wicked or that God has left you, and help is there.

memory_verse.text: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.

activity.title: The Stone and the Field
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s picture of his sin as “this little clot or stone” compared with “this vast and wide field.”
Ask everyone to draw it for themselves: a tiny stone in a huge field, with 1 John 1:7 written across the field.
Discuss the question the chapter raises: was one tired, panicked thought after a year of resistance really the same as choosing to reject Jesus?
Talk about why arguing alone with a thought on a loop rarely works, and why telling someone safe is not giving in but getting help.
Encourage anyone stuck in a mental argument to talk privately to you or another trusted adult this week.

weeks.summary: Convinced he has committed the unforgivable sin, Bunyan compares himself with David, Peter and Judas, feels like a burden and terror to himself, “weary of my life, and yet afraid to die,” and is shaken by the story of Francis Spira. He decides to pray anyway, at the foot of Christ, and when the first older Christian he confides in agrees with his fear, he goes back to God rather than giving up. He later realises his terror came from misunderstanding his sin. The big idea: dark feelings can be real while their conclusion is wrong, so keep praying and keep telling safe people.

memory_verse.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

activity.title: Ready to Help
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s decision: “I can but die; and if it must be so, it shall once be said, that such an one died at the foot of Christ in prayer.”

Discuss the three lessons the chapter gives: you are not the first to feel this, if the first person you tell gets it wrong tell someone else, and feelings can be real while their conclusion is wrong.
As a group, find the crisis line number for your country and have everyone save it in their phone or write it down.
Talk through what a good friend might say and do if someone told them they didn’t want to be here, including telling a trusted adult.
Close by reminding everyone that you are available to talk privately, and that they can come to you this week.

weeks.summary: Sitting on a bench, Bunyan hears, “This sin is not unto death,” and later, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love.” When the tempter says prayer is useless, he keeps answering, “Yet I will pray.” The words “My grace is sufficient for thee” grow until they outweigh the verse about Esau, and he clings to Jesus’ promise, “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out,” meaning any him. The big idea: healing may be a slow tipping of the scales, but God’s words, not our feelings, are what we hold on to.

memory_verse.text: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

activity.title: Yet I Will Pray
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s exchange with the tempter, ending each time with “Yet, said I, I will pray.”
Discuss why Bunyan’s healing came like scales tipping back and forth rather than one bright moment.
Give everyone a card and ask them to choose one of Bunyan’s two verses, 2 Corinthians 12:9 or John 6:37, and write it out.
Practise saying both verses together a few times.
Encourage everyone to learn their verse by heart this week and use it to answer doubts the way Bunyan did.

weeks.summary: Bunyan finds comfort in the cities of refuge for those who killed by accident, and when he finally reads the frightening verses in Hebrews carefully, they no longer look so grim. Walking in a field he hears, “Thy righteousness is in heaven,” and sees that his righteousness is Christ himself, unchanged by his good or bad moods; his chains fall off. He also reflects on what he learned from his long trial. The big idea: our standing with God does not rise and fall with our mood; it rests on Christ.

memory_verse.text: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.

activity.title: Gold in the Trunk
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s picture of the small coins in his pocket and the gold in his trunk at home.
Discuss what the coins and the gold stand for in his picture.
Talk about why it helped Bunyan to read the frightening verses in Hebrews in context, and why it is wise to do that with someone, not alone.
Give everyone a card to write out 1 Corinthians 1:30.
Encourage them to read it on a day they feel far from God and say: my righteousness is not my mood today; it is Christ.

weeks.summary: The Bedford church asks Bunyan to preach, and crowds come; he preaches first about sin from his own experience, “in chains to them in chains,” and later about Christ. He loves those who come to faith, still faces temptations and pride while preaching, and reminds himself that a cymbal makes no music by itself: “great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace.” He answers false rumours by denying them and treating them as an ornament. The big idea: God uses broken people before they are fixed, and grace matters more than gifts.

memory_verse.text: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.

activity.title: Great Grace, Small Gifts
steps: Read aloud “great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace.”
Ask everyone to write down, for themselves, two or three gifts they have, from music to listening to fixing things.
In pairs, have teens think of one quiet way to use one of those gifts for someone else this week.
Discuss the cymbal picture: where does the music really come from?
Challenge everyone to use one gift quietly this week and thank God for it rather than waiting for praise.

weeks.summary: Arrested in 1660 for preaching, Bunyan refuses to promise silence and spends twelve years in Bedford gaol, grieving for his wife Elizabeth and four children, especially his blind daughter Mary. Fearing he might be hanged and feeling nothing of God, he resolves to “leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity,” trusting Christ to catch him. Prison gives him his closest time with God’s word; he writes this book, later The Pilgrim’s Progress, and ends still honest about his struggles. The big idea: what keeps us safe is not our hold on God but his hold on us.

memory_verse.text: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.

activity.title: If Thou Wilt Catch Me
steps: Read aloud Bunyan’s words about leaping off the ladder blindfold.
Discuss the cost his choice brought to his family, which the chapter does not hide.
Talk about what it means that Bunyan’s hold on God was never what kept him safe, but God’s hold on him.
Give everyone a few minutes to write a short honest prayer of their own, beginning “Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do,” naming one fear and one person they want to trust God with.
Encourage them to pray it every day this week.
